Non-blocking. 'Platelets also make ... thromboxane A2': c-pgi2-1 says only that TXA2 'pushes the other way'. It does not say platelets make it. That fact is in c-txa2-1 / c-cox-1, which this paragraph does not cite. The content is correct.
correction: Add c-txa2-1 (or c-cox-1) to claims, or change to 'Another signal, thromboxane A2, pushes the other way.'

detail: Non-blocking. 'It takes a break in the lining to start one' is absolute. c-endo-1's simplified note says the absence of activating factors also matters. Clinically, clots can also form inside vessels without an obvious break (for example, a DVT from stasis). That belongs in a later module, but the absolute wording should be softened now.
correction: In normal hemostasis, it takes a break in the lining to start one.

BLOCKING (overstatement, safety-relevant). c-plug-2 says these problems 'typically' cause skin and mucosal bleeding. The lesson upgrades that to 'a signature'. The cited sp-petechiae passage itself says petechiae and purpura also come from coagulation disorders and loss of vascular integrity, so the finding does not point only to platelets. On scene, 'signature = skin and mucosa' can lead an EMT to underrate a patient with very low or non-working platelets (including those on antiplatelet drugs). Those patients can also bleed internally, for example GI bleeding or bleeding inside the skull after a minor head bump.
correction: Platelet problems typically show as bleeding into the skin and the moist linings of the body: petechiae (pinpoint spots), purpura, easy bruising, nosebleeds, and bleeding gums. These signs can have other causes too. (If an internal-bleeding warning is wanted, add a sourced claim first.)

detail: Non-blocking. All numbers are correct and supported by c-pc-1 and c-pc-2. However, 'mild drops' has no number, and a learner may read 50,000-80,000 as 'mild'. c-pc-2 defines mild as 100,000-150,000. The source also says counts above 50,000 usually cause no symptoms, so the 20,000-50,000 middle band is left undefined.
correction: Mild drops (100,000 to 150,000) usually cause no symptoms. Very low counts, under about 10,000 to 20,000, can bleed with no injury at all.

detail: Correct and supported by c-vwd-1 and c-pc-3. 'Typically normal' properly covers the vWD subtypes in which the count is low. The point that a normal count doesn't prove platelets work is clinically valuable.
Bernard-Soulier (GPIb, adhesion) and Glanzmann (GPIIb/IIIa, aggregation) are correctly matched and supported by c-gpib-2 and c-gp2-3.
Mechanism correct; supported by c-asa-1.
Supported by c-cox-2 and c-asa-2. It correctly says the effect fades only as platelets are replaced and does not depend on drug levels in the blood. The duration is not understated.

BLOCKING (small wording fix; duration framed as ending sooner than the sources say). The mechanism, irreversibility and prodrug status are correct (c-clop-1, c-clop-2, c-pras-1). Problems: (1) Unlike the aspirin paragraph, this one never says that each blocked platelet stays blocked for its whole 7-10 day life, although c-clop-3 and c-pras-1 both say so. (2) 'Generally within about 5 days' turns the label's 'generally in about 5 days' into an upper limit; the other source says only 'often seen within 5 days'. Together, these could make an EMT think Plavix wears off faster or more completely than aspirin. They could also make a patient who stopped 4-5 days ago seem to have normal platelets. 'ADP can't switch on GPIIb/IIIa' is slightly absolute (ADP still acts through P2Y1, and TXA2 and thrombin still work), but it matches c-clop-1 and is acceptable.
correction: Clopidogrel (Plavix) and prasugrel (Effient) permanently block P2Y12, so ADP can't switch on GPIIb/IIIa. Both start as inactive prodrugs that the body has to convert. Like aspirin, each blocked platelet stays blocked for its whole 7-to-10-day life. After the last dose, function comes back only gradually as new platelets are made: generally in about 5 days for clopidogrel, and over about 5 to 9 days for prasugrel.

detail: Supported by c-tica-1. 'Reversible doesn't mean short' is the right safety framing, and the roughly 5-day label figure is correctly stated.
